title: The fire of anger
hookLine: don't be angry, said three times (Bukhari)

cards: A man comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with a simple request. Advise me. Not a question about law, or the end of the world.
Just something to carry. The answer is short. Don't be angry.
The man asks again, maybe hoping for something bigger. Don't be angry. He asks again.
The same answer, every time. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the whole exchange, repetitions and all. Today's word: ghadab, anger.

teach.b: First, what the advice can't mean. Anger arrives on its own; nobody chooses the first flash. So the hadith is about what happens next.

Another hadith in al-Bukhari makes that plain: the strong one isn't the one who throws people in wrestling, but the one who controls himself when he's angry. Strength, moved from the arms to the moment after the flash.

Second, the Qur'an praises those who do exactly that, in Pickthall's words: "those who control their wrath and are forgiving toward mankind." Control first, then forgiveness. Anger isn't denied; it's held.
Third, the body. Reports in Sunan Abu Dawud give practical steps.

If you're angry while standing, sit down; if it hasn't left, lie down. Another says anger comes from Satan, Satan was made from fire, and fire is put out with water, so when angry, make wudu, the washing before prayer.
And in al-Bukhari, when two men were quarreling and one's face had gone red, the Prophet said he knew words that would take it away: seeking refuge in Allah from Satan. Lower the body. Cool the skin.
Say the words. Last, why it's called a fire. Fire spreads, and it's hard to call back; what's said in anger tends to outlast the anger.

teach.h: BETWEEN THE SPARK AND WHAT IT CATCHES.
teach.b: The short advice gets between the spark and whatever it would catch.

how: Muslims are taught to answer anger by sitting or lying down, making wudu, and seeking refuge in Allah from Satan, following hadith reports; restraining anger and forgiving are praised in the Qur'an.

o: any strong feeling, joy or sorrow alike
a curse spoken against someone in a fight
anger: the heat the hadith says to hold and cool

games.q: the fire of anger — tap the pairs.

s: in the hadith, the strong one is the best wrestler
the strong one controls himself when he's angry.
the Qur'an praises those who control their wrath
"those who control their wrath and are forgiving toward mankind."
the man in the hadith got a long list of advice
he asked again and again, and the answer stayed the same: don't be angry.

games.q: two men are quarreling; one's face has gone red. what did the Prophet say would take the anger away?
o: seeking refuge in Allah from Satan.
games.why: he said he knew words that would take it away: seeking refuge in Allah from Satan (Sahih al-Bukhari).

practice: Let a small annoyance come to mind, a slow driver, a message left on read, and notice where the heat starts: chest, face, hands.
Feel the chair under you holding your weight; you're already doing the first step, sitting, and if water is near later, you can cool your hands and face.
If you pray, you can seek refuge in Allah from Satan, as in the hadith; if not, just let the heat cool.

wordCard.voice: Ghadab. Anger; the fire the hadith answers with sitting, water and refuge in Allah. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: don't be angry. The flash comes on its own; what comes next is yours. That's today, done.
